summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual activity is lawful in Peru under the 1924 Penal Code; the 1863 code had criminalised sodomy with penalties comparable to those for rape. The age of consent is 14 irrespective of gender or sexual orientation, following a 2012 Constitutional Court decision, and applies to trans and cisgender youth alike. Trans identity is not itself an offence.

No legal protection against discrimination or hate crime on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is in force. Government Decree Nº 1323 criminalised such discrimination with effect from 7 January 2017 through Articles 46 and 323 of the Penal Code. Congress voted 66 to 29 in May 2017 to strip those provisions, after an April Constitutional Committee vote and a petition for removal carrying one million signatures; the repeal was carried by Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members, who argued the President lacked authority to issue the decree. President Kuczynski's veto stood at that point, and the protections were removed as the Penal Code was reworked. Peru is one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, without LGBT anti-discrimination coverage.

Law 32331, enacted 13 May 2025, bars trans people from using public restrooms matching their gender identity. It followed the April 2025 "Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents", which requires restroom entry to be determined by "biological sex" and prohibits inclusive signage such as "women in their diversity". The measures originated in bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR, presented by congressmen Muñante and Montoya; in February 2025 a congressional committee approved unanimously for plenary the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457, presented by Jorge Montoya and the Honor y Democracia party. Human Rights Watch reports that vague child-protection articles, article 4 on media and advertising and article 5, permit censorship of identity, artistic and educational content, and that the minimum sentence for obscenity offences rose from three to four years.

The human-rights institute at the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru (IDEHPUCP) assesses the restroom provision as open discrimination against trans and non-binary people, implicitly framing them as harassment risks. It cites Inter-American Court of Human Rights Advisory Opinion OC-24/17, which holds that gender identity falls within protected personal autonomy and obliges states to guarantee trans people's full rights. The institute also quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons. The restroom law is a state-imposed restriction on trans people's daily movement that can intensify hostile encounters in transit spaces.

Trans Peruvians may change their legal name to match their gender identity. In 2014 the Constitutional Court barred gender-marker changes on national identity documents, then reversed itself in a ruling of 21 October 2016 published on 8 November, permitting a gender change through a judicial process without sex-reassignment surgery. A Gender Identity Law, introduced on 4 November 2016, would allow legal gender change without surgery and access to passports and other identity documents matching gender identity; it remained pending in the legislature as of March 2021. There is no self-declaration procedure.

In May 2024 the government decreed "transsexualism" a mental health problem in order to cover trans healthcare; after protests, in June 2024 the Ministry of Health revised the term to "gender discordance" for health-insurance classification. Human Rights Watch reported in June 2024 that health authorities had removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance. In May 2024 the ministry reiterated that sexual orientation and gender identity are not diseases. Conversion therapy is banned for medical professionals.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years in prison for the torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist, nearly 20 years after the attack. It is Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case. Monitoring organisations report that trans women are the group most affected by hate crimes in the country.

Outright International records that public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, ruling on an activist legal challenge, found an anti-equality decree unconstitutional. An April 2025 law on foreign funding of NGOs allows authorities to revoke registrations on "public order or security" grounds, creating a route to act against queer organising.

Organisations working on trans rights list unmet demands including equal marriage and recognition of diverse families, alongside HIV medication supply, revision of outdated medical rules, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.
tangentialFactors:
Willax TV presenter Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian congresswoman, telling her to use the men's room. Congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at the National Maternal Perinatal Institute (INMP), an adjacent front in the same legislative push.

Opinion polling shows age-based variation in attitudes: 66% of 18 to 24-year-olds were favourable toward homosexuals against 49% of the population overall, and approval of same-sex marriage stood at 8.3% in 2010, higher among younger respondents.
localsOnly:
A 2012 study by Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia found that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao worked in sex work, a figure that describes the economic position of resident trans women rather than visitors.

Pride marches have been held annually since 2002, with the oldest recorded march in 1984. The 2016 national education curriculum includes material on sexual orientation, sex and gender, describing sexual orientation as the product of complex biological, cognitive and environmental circumstances and not a voluntary choice.
outOfScopeNotes:
Official hate-crime counts are described by monitoring organisations as a sub-registry, so no reliable magnitude of trans-specific violence in Peru can be stated from the available figures.

The current status of the Gender Identity Law after March 2021 is not sourced. Whether the restroom restriction is being enforced in practice, and how, is not documented in the available material.
